title: Night Flight 2
content:
It used to be that people came to him asking what to do. Now, he was the one asking others, completely lost, with no idea where to turn. And there wasn't a single soul who could give him an answer.

Suddenly, a tiny prick of pain flared at the side of Wei Wuxian’s neck—like the sting of an impossibly slender needle. A wave of numbness instantly washed through him. His mind had been so scrambled, his guard so completely down, that by the time he realized something was wrong, his body was already tipping sideways onto the stone bed. He tried to raise an arm, but before he could even lift it halfway, it dropped dead against the slab. He was paralyzed from the neck down.

Eyes rimmed in red, Wen Qing slowly pulled her right hand back. "...I'm sorry."

Under normal circumstances, she wouldn't have stood a chance of landing a needle on him, but Wei Wuxian had been completely defenseless. The puncture hit deep, shocking his scattered thoughts into a chilling stillness. His throat hitched, his Adam's apple bobbing before he managed to force out, "What the hell are you doing?"

Wen Qing and Wen Ning exchanged a solemn glance. Stepping up side-by-side before him, they bowed in deep, formal unison.

The sight made a surge of frantic panic claw at Wei Wuxian’s chest. "What are you doing?! What is this?!"

Wen Qing said evenly, "When you woke up, we were just finishing our discussion. It's settled."

"Settled what?! Cut the crap! Pull the needle out and let me go!"

Wen Ning slowly pushed himself up from the floor, keeping his chin tucked low. "Jiejie and I... we made up our minds. We're going to Koi Tower. To surrender."

"Surrender?!" Wei Wuxian gasped, stunned. "Surrender what? Turn yourselves in? Offer yourselves up on a silver platter?!"

Wen Qing rubbed her swollen eyes, her voice forced into a brittle, calm facade. "Pretty much. While you were out cold these past few days, the Lanling Jin Sect sent runners to the foot of the mountain with an ultimatum."

"What ultimatum?! Stop speaking in riddles! Tell me the whole thing, right now!"

Wen Qing replied, "Lanling Jin demands accountability. And that means handing over the two ringleaders of the Wen remnants. Especially the Ghost General."

Wei Wuxian went dead silent for a beat. "I'm warning both of you. Pull. This needle. Out."

Wen Qing barreled on, deaf to the threat: "The ringleaders are just the two of us anyway. From the sound of it, as long as you toss them our heads, they'll let the rest of this blow over for now. So do us a favor and stay in bed a few more days. That needle's good for three days before the paralysis wears off. I gave Fourth Uncle and the others strict orders to watch over you. If shit hits the fan before the three days are up, they'll pull you out."

Fury detonated in his chest. "Shut the fuck up! It's already an absolute disaster out there! Stop making it worse! Surrender? What kind of bullshit self-righteous stunt is that?! Did I tell you to do that?! Pull it out!"

The siblings stood with their arms hanging limp, wrapped in the exact same stubborn, suffocating silence. Wei Wuxian’s body was dead weight. The harder he strained against the paralysis to no avail, the colder the dread pooling in his gut became. When nobody listens, screaming gets you nowhere.

Unable to shout, unable to twitch, his voice cracked into a hoarse rasp: "What are you even going to Koi Tower for? That Hundred Holes curse had nothing to do with me...!"

"Doesn't matter," Wen Qing cut in. "They've already decided it was you."

Wei Wuxian scrambled for an out, a sudden lightbulb flicking on. "Then we track down the bastard who actually cast it! Jin Zixun had to have consulted curse-masters, and the standard play for a blood curse is reflecting it back on the caster! Even if you can't bounce the whole thing, part of it always rebounds! We just need to search for whoever’s walking around with the same curse marks on their flesh!"

Wen Qing sighed. "It's useless."

"Why the hell is it useless?!"

"Where are you going to start looking? Comb through the entire empire? Set up checkpoints on every highway in every province, stripping every cultivator bare for an inspection?"

"Why not?!" Wei Wuxian babbled frantically. "Why the hell can't we?!"

Wen Qing countered, "Who’s going to help you build those checkpoints? And how long will it take? Maybe you find them in eight or ten years—do you think they’re going to wait that long for you?"

"I don't have rebound marks on my body!"

"Did they bother asking to check before they tried to butcher you today?"

Wei Wuxian choked. "...No."

"Exactly. No questions, just cold steel," she said, stripping away his illusions. "See? They don't need proof, and they sure as hell don't want you digging up the truth. Whether you have marks on your skin doesn't mean shit. You're the Yiling Laozu. You rule the crooked path. You invented the dark arts—why would it shock anyone if you figured out a way to dodge the backlash? Hell, you wouldn't even have to cast it yourself; you could've just ordered one of your Wen lapdogs to do the dirty work. At the end of the day, it's pinned on you. You can't wash it off."

Wei Wuxian let out a strangled curse.

Wen Qing waited quietly for the vitriol to die down before driving the knife home: "So face it. It's over. And honestly, at this point, who cast the Hundred Holes doesn't matter anymore. What matters is that the three hundred men at Qiongqi Path... and Jin Zixuan... A-Ning really did kill them."

Wei Wuxian sputtered, "...B-But... But..."

But what? He couldn't even invent a 'but' to save his life. No excuses left. No loopholes to hide behind.

"...If anyone goes," he choked out, "it should be me. I was the one pulling the strings. Since when does the court put the sword on trial instead of the killer?"

Wen Qing’s voice softened. "Isn't this better?"

"Better how?! How the hell is this better?!"

"Wei Ying, let's be real," she said, her tone heartbreakingly flat. "Wen Ning is a weapon. He's a blade that terrifies them, but he's also the exact excuse they're using to come for your throat. If we walk into Koi Tower, you lose that blade. And when you don't have it anymore, they lose their excuse. Maybe then... this whole nightmare finally ends."

Wei Wuxian stared at her, dumbfounded, before a raw, wordless roar tore through his chest.

In that split second, he finally understood Jiang Cheng. He understood why Jiang Cheng looked at him with incandescent rage, why he constantly screamed that Wei Wuxian had a martyr complex, why he always looked on the verge of beating him bloody just to knock some sense into his skull. Watching someone stubbornly hoard all the blame, watching them march headfirst into a meat grinder while completely ignoring every plea to stop—it was sickening. It made you want to claw your own eyes out.

"Do you two have any idea what you're walking into?!" Wei Wuxian spat, his voice shaking. "Turning yourselves in at Koi Tower—what do you think they're going to do to you? Especially Wen Ning?! Aren't you supposed to treasure your brother more than your own life?!"

Wen Qing replied evenly, "Whatever happens to him, he brought it on himself."

No. It wasn't Wen Ning who brought it on himself. It was Wei Wuxian.

Wen Qing continued, "Besides, strictly speaking, we should have been dead a long time ago. These past few months... we consider them borrowed time."

Beside her, Wen Ning gave a slow nod.

Always like this. Whatever anyone said, he just nodded along, agreeable to a fault, never putting up a fight. Wei Wuxian had never despised that meek compliance more than he did right now.

Wen Qing dropped into a crouch beside the stone slab, studying his face. Out of nowhere, her fingers flicked, snapping a sharp, stinging thwack right against his forehead.

The flick carried real force, pulling a sharp grimace from his brow. Catching the scowl, Wen Qing’s features seemed to ease, a faint, bittersweet warmth touching her lips. "Alright. Everything's said, debts are settled, and we said our goodbyes. So... farewell."

"Don't..." Wei Wuxian gasped, but she cut him off cleanly.

"I haven't said this to your face much, but today's the day for it. Won't get another shot after this."

"Shut up..." he mumbled, panic thick in his throat. "Let me go..."

Wen Qing looked down at him. "I'm sorry. And... thank you."

Wei Wuxian lay paralyzed on that stone bed for three entire days.

Her arithmetic was terrifyingly precise. Exactly three days down to the second—not a moment more, not a moment less—the numbness finally broke.

First his fingers twitched, then his limbs, then his neck. The moment his sluggish, freezing blood rushed back through his veins, Wei Wuxian launched himself off the stone, bolting out of the Demon-Subduing Cave like a shot.

The remaining Wen remnants looked as though they hadn't slept a wink either, huddled in absolute silence around the tables beneath the great timber shelter. Wei Wuxian didn't spare them a single glance, sprinting down the rocky paths of the Burial Mounds as if pursued by demons.

Bursting through the perimeter, he hit the desolate flats below, bent double, wheezing for air with his hands clamped to his knees. It took several agonizing seconds just to drag his spine straight. But staring down at the tangled, overgrown forks in the road, he froze.

He had no idea where to go.

The Burial Mounds? He’d just scrambled down from that rock.

Lotus Pier? He hadn't stepped foot in his home in over a year.

Koi Tower?

Three full days had slipped by. If he marched on Koi Tower now, the only things waiting for him would be Wen Qing’s cold corpse and Wen Ning’s ashes.

He stood rooted in the weeds, a sudden, suffocating vertigo crashing down upon him. The world was impossibly vast, yet there wasn't a single patch of dirt left on it that would have him.

He didn't even know what he was supposed to do next.

Then, out of the darkest recess of his soul, a vile, monstrous thought bubbled to the surface.

A thought he’d spent the last three days violently beating down, only for it to crawl right back up like an inescapable phantom.

Wen Qing and Wen Ning went on their own.

Deep down... was he relieved?

Relieved that he didn't have to make an impossible choice anymore? Because they had stepped up, taken the burden off his shoulders, and made the decision for him?

Smack!

Wei Wuxian reared back and slapped himself across the face with everything he had, his own snarl tearing through his teeth: "What the fuck is wrong with you?!"

The stinging heat radiating across his cheek finally crushed the poison back into the dirt. Shifting his thoughts, he latched onto a singular resolve: no matter what, he had to bring their bodies—or whatever ashes remained—back home.

He took off at a dead run, heading straight for Koi Tower.

For someone of Wei Wuxian’s caliber, slipping into an estate undetected was child's play. Yet Koi Tower was eerily, deathly quiet—none of the ironclad patrols or paranoid cordons he’d braced for. He spent half the afternoon ghosting through the perimeter, turning up nothing suspicious.

He drifted through the sprawling palace courtyards like a wraith, dodging wherever someone approached, slipping through the shadows when the corridors emptied. He didn't even know what he was hunting for, or how he was supposed to find it. But when the thin, fragile wail of an infant drifted through the night air, his boots locked up. An invisible cord yanked at his marrow, driving his feet toward the sound.

The weeping seeped from a cavernous, pitch-black hall.

Gliding to the threshold without a whisper of sound, Wei Wuxian peered through the delicate lattice of the carved wooden shutters.

In the center of the hall rested a massive, pitch-black coffin. Kneeling before it were two women draped in mourning white.

The one on the left was frail, her frame heartbreakingly slender. He could never mistake that back. From childhood until now, he had been carried on those shoulders countless times.

It was Jiang Yanli.

She knelt upon a rush mat, staring blankly at the lacquered dark wood of the casket before her. Cradled against her chest was the child, letting out soft, reedy whimpers.

The woman to her right spoke in a hushed murmur: "...A-Li, please. Stop kneeling here. Go rest."

Jiang Yanli gave a tiny, numb shake of her head. Madame Jin let out a long, ragged sigh.

She was a woman cut from the exact same cloth as her late friend Madam Yu—proud, unyielding, her voice usually pitched with sharp, regal authority. Yet the words slipping from her lips now were raspy, cracked, and infinitely old.

"I can keep vigil here," Madame Jin coaxed softly. "If you keep sitting like this, your body will break."

Jiang Yanli whispered, "Mother, I'm fine. I just... want to sit a little longer."

After a heavy pause, Madame Jin slowly pushed herself up. "You can't keep carrying on like this. I'll fetch you something warm to eat."

She had clearly spent hours on her knees; her joints had seized, her balance wobbling the second she stood, though she steadied herself instantly. Turning toward the light, the sharp, aristocratic lines of her face came into view.

The Madame Jin living in Wei Wuxian’s memory had been an untouchable tempest—arrogant, dazzling, draped in shimmering gold and radiating unassailable wealth. She had maintained her beauty with ruthless care, looking youthful enough that passing strangers easily mistook her for a woman in her early twenties. Yet standing before him now was an ordinary, grieving middle-aged woman draped in unadorned funeral linen, frost threading heavily through the gray at her temples. No makeup. Her face was ashen, her lips cracked with dry, peeling skin.

She turned to push the doors open. Wei Wuxian reacted on pure instinct, leaping lightly into the air and tucking himself up into the structural eaves of the veranda. The heavy doors creaked open; Madame Jin stepped through, pulling them shut behind her. She stood on the walkway, drew in a long, shuddering breath, and worked her jaw, fighting to reconstruct her trademark mask of cold authority.

Before that breath could finish filling her lungs, her eyes went violently bloodshot.

Inside, in front of Jiang Yanli, she hadn't allowed a single fracture of grief to show. But the second she stepped into the private dark, the corners of her mouth collapsed, her features knotting into a raw, trembling grimace as violent sobs shook her entire frame.

This was the second time Wei Wuxian had watched a woman's face twist into an expression so hideous—and so utterly heartbroken.

He never, ever wanted to witness that look again.

Without realizing it, Wei Wuxian clenched his fist.

Crack.

The tiny pop of a knuckle echoed through the quiet. Madame Jin’s brow snapped into a vicious arch. "Who's there?!"

She whipped her head up, her gaze locking dead onto Wei Wuxian crouching in the shadows of the eaves. Her vision was razor-sharp; the second she made out the face hidden in the dark, her expression contorted in pure, hysterical horror.

"Guards!" she shrieked, her voice tearing through the rafters. "Someone get out here! Wei Ying—he's here! He infiltrated Koi Tower!"

Wei Wuxian dropped from the eaves, landing on the stones. Urgent, frantic footfalls scrambled from inside the hall; someone was running for the doors. Panic seizing his throat, he turned and fled.

Right now, he didn't have the stomach to face Jiang Yanli. He couldn't bear to see her look at him—let alone hear whatever words she might say.

Breaking through Koi Tower's perimeter and slipping past the gates of Lanling City, Wei Wuxian lost all sense of direction. He wandered blindly through the backcountry, his head an incoherent, buzzing static, boots trudging without pause. He had no idea how many provinces he’d crossed when a bustling crowd gathered before a city wall caught his attention, voices loud, furious, and thick with righteous clamor.

He would have walked right past them, but as he drifted by, the words "Ghost General" floated through the noise. His boots stopped cold.

"The Ghost General really is an absolute monster... Claimed he went there to surrender, then suddenly lost his mind and went on another slaughter spree right on Koi Tower!"

"Thank the gods I skipped that banquet!"

"A stray dog trained by Wei Wuxian—snapping at anyone in sight."

"Wei Ying is an idiot. If you can't control your own toys, don't invent them in the first place! Forging a rabid hound and letting it off the leash—it's only a matter of time before it turns on him. Judging by this mess, that day's right around the corner."

Wei Wuxian stood in the shadows, muscles twitching along his jaw, knuckles cracking silently.

"The Lanling Jin Sect really drew the short straw."

"The Gusu Lan Clan got it worse! More than half of the thirty-odd casualties belonged to their house, and they were only there to keep the peace and cool tempers!"

"Well, at least the Ghost General was finally incinerated to dust. The thought of that thing roaming the wild, throwing tantrums whenever he felt like it... kept me up at night."

Someone spat, "Wen dogs got exactly what they had coming!"

"Now that the monster's been reduced to ash, Wei Wuxian ought to know his place. I hear several clan leaders heading to the rally have already sworn blood oaths. Good riddance!"

The longer Wei Wuxian listened, the colder the numbness on his face became.

He should have seen this coming. No matter what he did, nothing good would ever spill from their mouths. When he soared, they cowered in terror; when he bled, they reveled in the spectacle.

At the end of the day, it was all "crooked heretical evil." So what the hell was the point of holding the line all this time? What was he even fighting for?

Yet the more arctic the chill in his gaze became, the hotter the furious, infernal fire roared behind his ribs.

A cultivator puffed his chest out, preening as though he personally held the credit: "Serves him right! If he knows what's good for him, he'll tuck his tail between his legs and rot on that cursed mountain for the rest of his miserable days. If he dares crawl out into the light again? Ha! The second he shows his face, we'll—"

"You'll do what?"

The lively debate cut out instantly. Every head whipped around.

Standing right behind them was a young man in black robes, his face ghost-pale, heavy charcoal shadows bruising the skin beneath his eyes. He stared down at them, his voice arctic: "The second he shows his face, you'll do what?"

A sharp-eyed disciple caught sight of the dark bamboo flute tucked into his sash, its crimson tassel swaying in the wind. Pure terror detonated in his throat: "Chenqing... It's Chenqing!"

The Yiling Laozu... was actually standing right in front of them!

In a heartbeat, the crowd scrambled, screaming as they tore open a wide circle around him. Wei Wuxian brought his lips together, letting loose a sharp, piercing whistle.

A crushing weight slammed down upon the cultivators, plastering them flat against the cobblestones. Trembling in sheer horror, they craned their necks—only to find grotesque, blood-dripping wraiths pinned heavy across their backs!

Wei Wuxian strolled through the sea of groveling, paralyzed bodies, his pace casual, entirely unbothered. "My, my, what happened to all that bravado? Running your mouths behind my back like you owned the world, but the second I'm standing here, you're kissing the dirt?"

He strode up to the loudmouth who had spewed the foulest venom, raising a boot and stomping it squarely into the man's face. He let out a cold, sharp laugh. "Go on! Why quiet down now?! Come on, hero—what were you going to do to me?!"

The impact shattered the man's nasal bone, blood spraying across the pavers as he shrieked in agony. Several cultivators perched along the top of the city wall watched the carnage, desperate to intervene yet petrified to drop down, settling for screaming down from a safe distance: "W-Wei Ying! If you've got real backbone, why don't you take this fight to the great clans at the rally?! What kind of hero picks on low-level cultivators who can't even fight back?!"

Wei Wuxian loosed another short, sharp whistle. An invisible hand violently yanked the screaming cultivator clean off the battlements; he crashed onto the flagstones below, both legs snapping with a sickening crunch as his wails joined the chorus.

Amidst the symphony of screaming agony, Wei Wuxian’s expression didn't flicker by a fraction. "Low-level cultivators? So just because you're weak, I'm obligated to swallow your insults? If you've got the balls to talk shit, you'd better have the balls to take the beating. If you know you're nothing more than insignificant, worthless vermin, learn to keep your damn mouths shut!"

The courtyard fell dead as a graveyard, the survivors gray-faced and terrified to breathe.

When not another whisper dared surface, Wei Wuxian murmured with quiet satisfaction, "There. That's better."

He punctuated the thought with another brutal kick, caving in the teeth of the loudmouth beneath his boot!

Blood splattered the stone, the man passing out cold from sheer agony. Wei Wuxian looked down, dragging the bloody sole of his boot across the dirt, leaving a smeared red footprint.

"Still," he murmured smoothly, "you vermin got one thing right. Wasting my breath on scum like you is completely pointless. Want me to go find the great clans? Fine. I'll head over right now and settle the ledger once and for all."

He raised his eyes toward the massive parchment nailed to the city wall—the very proclamation the mob had been salivating over.

Emblazoned across the top were four large characters: GREAT PLEDGE RALLY.

The notice decreed that the Four Great Sects—Lanling Jin, Qinghe Nie, Yunmeng Jiang, and Gusu Lan—would gather atop the ruins of the Nightless City, the fallen seat of Qishan Wen. There, they would scatter the ashes of the Wen remnants to the wind, swearing a blood oath before heaven and earth to cleanse the realm of the Yiling Laozu once and for all.

Nightless City. A Great Pledge Rally.
